description: Question: four houses in Britain run the same model of air-source heat pump (Vaillant aroTHERM plus) through the same winter. Why does one get almost twice as much heat per kWh of electricity as another? Data: a year (November 2025 to October 2026) of daily, metered space-heating statistics per house from HeatpumpMonitor.org, OpenEnergyMonitor's open-data project (heat and electricity in kWh from heat and electricity meters, mean flow, return, outdoor and room temperatures): systems 802 (Cheshire, 10 kW, underfloor heating and radiators), 254 (Angus, 7 kW), 357 (Newcastle upon Tyne, 7 kW) and 700 (London, 7 kW), the last three with radiators; heating-season days (daily mean outdoor temperature up to 15 °C). Idea: the Carnot limit of a heat pump. Moving heat from cold air at T_cold to water at T_hot costs at least the work W = Q (1 − T_cold/T_hot), so the coefficient of performance COP = Q/W can never exceed T_hot/(T_hot − T_cold), in kelvin. It depends only on the lift T_hot − T_cold; a real machine reaches a roughly fixed share of it. Steps: each house's CSV to days (Polars); the four together with COP, lift and Carnot COP (SQL); COP per 2 K band of outdoor temperature; the year per house (seasonal COP, heat-weighted flow temperature and lift); least squares of COP on the Carnot COP and on the lift; the Carnot curves for 25–45 °C water. The aha: the four houses' days fall on one line, COP ≈ η × Carnot, and what separates them is the flow temperature, not the climate: the house with underfloor heating heats with water at 29 °C (heat-weighted) and reaches a seasonal COP of 5.66; the London house needs 38.5 °C and gets 3.92, though its winter is milder. Across all 1,039 heating days the COP is about 0.35 × Carnot (r = 0.77), and each kelvin of lift costs 0.16 in COP: 5 K lower flow temperature is worth about 17%. Bigger radiators, underfloor heating and weather compensation are thermodynamics, not marketing. Caveats: four self-selected, carefully run systems; space heating only (hot water runs at 45–55 °C and a lower COP); outdoor temperature from each unit's sensor; the 'Carnot' here uses the mean flow temperature and outdoor air, while the refrigerant runs a few kelvin hotter and colder (heatpumpmonitor.org's own %Carnot uses those offsets, so its numbers are higher); days with less than 0.5 kWh of electricity are dropped. HeatpumpMonitor.org publishes the data as open data for others to learn from; cite the site and the system ids. Next: open other systems by id (the public list holds hundreds with model, emitters and heat loss), or join Open-Meteo's archive at each house's location to check the outdoor sensor.
name: Heat pumps and the Carnot limit: why flow temperature matters
